children.title: Affine-Nonlinear Optimality Gap
children.top_down_role: Differences between affine-map and general nonexpansive-map optimality.

children.title: Affine-Map Optimality
children.top_down_role: Optimality behavior specific to affine fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Map Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual optimality over the affine Krylov information class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T(x)=Ax+b\), suppose \(I-A\) is nonsingular, and set \(r_0=x_0-Tx_0\). Every residual obtainable from the affine Krylov space \(x_0+\mathcal K_N(I-A,r_0)\) has the form \(q(A)r_0\), where \(q\) is a polynomial with \(\deg q\leq N\) and \(q(1)=1\). Consequently, an exact residual-minimizing Krylov extrapolation satisfies
\[
\lVert x_N-Tx_N\rVert
=
\min_{\substack{\deg q\leq N\\q(1)=1}}
\lVert q(A)r_0\rVert.
\]
Thus polynomial residual minimization is optimal within this affine information class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For affine fixed-point maps, Krylov extrapolation minimizes the residual over all admissible degree-N residual polynomials.
assumptions_latex: \(T(x)=Ax+b\) on a finite-dimensional normed inner-product space.
Computations use the affine Krylov space generated by \(r_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_N-Tx_N\rVert=\min_{\deg q\leq N,\ q(1)=1}\lVert q(A)r_0\rVert\).

notation.meaning: span of the first N Krylov vectors generated by M and r

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: affine fixed-point residual minimization is the corresponding linear-system Krylov polynomial problem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role is compatible with affine-map optimality, but no source supports the exact equivalence between the stated affine Krylov space and the normalization q(1)=1. The phrase “exact residual-minimizing Krylov extrapolation” also needs a cited definition of the method and norm.

children.title: General Nonexpansive-Map Optimality
children.top_down_role: Optimality behavior across unrestricted nonexpansive maps.

knowledge_statements.title: General Nonexpansive-Map Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax residual order over unrestricted nonexpansive maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal T_R\) be the class of nonexpansive maps \(T\) on Hilbert spaces for which the supplied initial point satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x_0,\operatorname{Fix}T)\leq R\). In the deterministic value-oracle model, the minimax residual after \(N\) evaluations obeys
\[
 c\frac{R}{N+1}
 \leq
 \inf_{\mathcal A_N}\sup_{T\in\mathcal T_R}
 \lVert z_N(T)-Tz_N(T)\rVert
 \leq
 C\frac{R}{N+1},
\]
for universal constants \(c,C>0\). Hence the sharp uniform decay order for general nonexpansive maps is \(\Theta(R/N)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimax fixed-point residual for deterministic value-oracle methods on general nonexpansive maps has exact order R/N.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) ranges over nonexpansive maps with a nonempty fixed-point set.
The initial distance to that set is at most \(R\).
Algorithms use at most \(N\) adaptive evaluations of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{\mathcal A_N}\sup_{T\in\mathcal T_R}\lVert z_N-Tz_N\rVert=\Theta(R/N)\).

notation.meaning: normalized class of nonexpansive fixed-point problems
deterministic algorithm using at most N oracle calls
output of the algorithm on map T

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: matching Halpern upper and adversarial nonexpansive lower bounds yield the minimax inverse-iteration order

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the general nonexpansive optimality leaf. The two-sided minimax statement nevertheless combines an upper bound and a strong adversarial oracle lower bound without a source specifying the common problem and oracle classes, so the claimed Theta order is not adequately supported.

children.title: Affine–Nonlinear Optimality Gap
children.top_down_role: Structural sources and consequences of the separation between the two map classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine–Nonlinear Optimality Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between affine polynomial acceleration and uniform nonlinear oracle guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-dimensional affine map \(T(x)=Ax+b\) with nonsingular \(I-A\), Krylov polynomial methods may terminate after the degree of the relevant minimal polynomial and can exploit spectral clustering before termination. This behavior does not extend as a uniform guarantee over all nonexpansive maps: after \(N\) value-oracle evaluations, an adversarial nonlinear nonexpansive map can still force residual at least \(cR/(N+1)\). Therefore affine finite termination or spectrum-dependent polynomial acceleration cannot be inferred from nonexpansiveness alone; affine linear structure is the missing assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine maps permit polynomial acceleration and finite termination, while unrestricted nonexpansive maps retain a worst-case inverse-iteration residual barrier.
assumptions_latex: Affine problems are finite-dimensional with \(I-A\) nonsingular.
The nonlinear comparison class contains all nonexpansive maps under a value oracle.
The initial fixed-point distance is bounded by \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Affine polynomial optimality does not imply a uniform rate better than \(\Theta(R/N)\) for general nonexpansive maps.

notation.meaning: linear part of an affine fixed-point map

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Krylov finite termination relies on affine polynomial structure absent from the general nonexpansive oracle class

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind correctly matches the affine–nonlinear gap container. Its comparison combines minimal-polynomial termination, spectral acceleration, and an oracle lower bound, none of which has an inspectable citation; the precise separation therefore remains source-dependent.

children.title: Local Acceleration Rate Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Local rate classifications for polynomial, multisecant, and residual-subspace accelerators.

children.title: Linear-Factor Improvement
children.top_down_role: Acceleration assessed through improved local contraction factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Factor Improvement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local acceleration measured per operator evaluation through the linearized residual polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_\star=T(x_\star)\), suppose \(T\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x_\star\), and write \(J=T'(x_\star)\). An \(m\)-step affine extrapolation whose coefficients sum to one has local error model
\[
e^+=p(J)e+o(\lVert e\rVert),
\qquad \deg p\leq m,
\qquad p(1)=1.
\]
If \(\lVert p(J)\rVert^{1/m}<\lVert J\rVert<1\), then its asymptotic linear contraction factor per operator evaluation is strictly smaller than that of the unaccelerated iteration. The improvement is local and depends on the chosen polynomial and linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extrapolation improves the local linear rate when its linearized residual polynomial has a smaller per-evaluation contraction factor than the base map.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is Fréchet differentiable at a fixed point \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert p(J)\rVert^{1/m}<\lVert J\rVert\) implies a strict local linear-factor improvement.

notation.meaning: derivative of the fixed-point map at the solution
polynomial induced by one extrapolation cycle

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local affine extrapolation acts polynomially on the derivative of the fixed-point map

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits local linear-factor improvement, but the displayed one-cycle model and the interpretation of its m-th root as a per-evaluation asymptotic factor require a precise extrapolation construction and local stability hypotheses. No authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Superlinear Multisecant Rates
children.top_down_role: Local fast-convergence regimes associated with improving multisecant models.

knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear Multisecant Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quasi-Newton superlinearity under a Dennis–Moré-type multisecant accuracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(F(x)=x-T(x)\). Suppose \(F\) is continuously differentiable near a zero \(x_\star\), \(F'(x_\star)\) is nonsingular, and a multisecant iteration has the form \(x_{k+1}=x_k-B_kF(x_k)\). If \(x_k\to x_\star\), the matrices \(B_k\) and \(B_k^{-1}\) remain bounded, and the accepted steps \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\) satisfy
\[
\frac{\lVert(B_k^{-1}-F'(x_\star))s_k\rVert}{\lVert s_k\rVert}\longrightarrow0,
\]
then the convergence is q-superlinear:
\[
\frac{\lVert x_{k+1}-x_\star\rVert}{\lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert}\longrightarrow0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent multisecant fixed-point method is q-superlinear when its inverse models satisfy a Dennis–Moré accuracy condition along accepted steps.
assumptions_latex: \(F=x-T\) is continuously differentiable and \(F'(x_\star)\) is nonsingular.
The displayed Dennis–Moré condition holds for nonzero accepted steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_\star\rVert/\lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert\to0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Dennis–Moré conditions characterize local superlinear quasi-Newton behavior

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the terminal container. The exact Dennis–Moré implication, including the required smoothness, nonsingularity, boundedness, nonzero-step, and multisecant assumptions, must be checked against an authoritative theorem; no citation is provided.

children.title: Polynomial Finite-Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exact-arithmetic linear regimes governed by finite-dimensional polynomial structure.

children.title: Minimal-Polynomial Structure
children.top_down_role: Finite-dimensional polynomial features governing accelerated linear iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Polynomial Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial representation governing affine fixed-point extrapolation and exact recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T(x)=Ax+b\) have a unique fixed point \(x_\star\), and set \(e_0=x_0-x_\star\). Let \(m_{A,e_0}\) be the monic polynomial of least degree \(d\) such that \(m_{A,e_0}(A)e_0=0\). Since \(I-A\) is nonsingular, \(m_{A,e_0}(1)\neq0\), and
\[
q(z)=\frac{m_{A,e_0}(z)}{m_{A,e_0}(1)}
\]
satisfies \(q(1)=1\) and \(q(A)e_0=0\). Hence the coefficients of \(q\) define an affine combination of \(x_0,T x_0,\ldots,T^d x_0\) whose value is exactly \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal polynomial relative to the initial error yields normalized affine coefficients that exactly recover the fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(T(x)=Ax+b\) acts on a finite-dimensional vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized relative minimal polynomial satisfies \(q(1)=1\) and \(q(A)e_0=0\), producing exact affine recovery.

notation.meaning: initial error relative to the fixed point
minimal polynomial of A relative to the initial error
degree of the relative minimal polynomial

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relative minimal-polynomial annihilation gives the classical exact affine extrapolation identity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the minimal-polynomial structure leaf, and the statement is algebraically plausible. An inspectable linear-algebra or extrapolation source is still required for the relative minimal-polynomial normalization and exact affine-recovery formulation.

children.title: Finite-Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem classes where exact-arithmetic acceleration reaches termination in finitely many terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Termination Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact termination of full Krylov residual minimization for affine fixed-point equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T(x)=Ax+b\), assume \(I-A\) is nonsingular, and let \(d\) be the degree of the minimal polynomial of \(A\) relative to \(e_0=x_0-x_\star\). In exact arithmetic, any residual-minimizing method that at step \(k\) searches the full affine Krylov space \(x_0+\mathcal K_k(I-A,x_0-Tx_0)\) and does not break down reaches zero residual in at most \(d\) steps:
\[
x_d-Tx_d=0,
\qquad x_d=x_\star.
\]
Thus finite termination requires finite-dimensional affine dynamics, full polynomial freedom, and exact realization of the Krylov minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full residual-minimizing Krylov acceleration terminates within the relative minimal-polynomial degree for nonsingular affine fixed-point equations in exact arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: The method minimizes over the full current affine Krylov space without breakdown.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_d=x_\star\) and \(x_d-Tx_d=0\) for some \(d\) no larger than the relative minimal-polynomial degree.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Krylov finite termination follows from relative minimal-polynomial annihilation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits finite-termination regimes. The phrase “any residual-minimizing method” is method-class sensitive, and the step count depends on the Krylov indexing and breakdown convention. These details require a specific GMRES/Krylov theorem citation.

children.title: Exact-Arithmetic Validity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of polynomial termination behavior to perturbations, rounding, or structural mismatch.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Arithmetic Validity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polynomial termination is not robust to perturbations or loss of affine structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The identity \(q(A)e_0=0\) implies finite termination only when the affine iterates and polynomial coefficients are formed exactly. If operator evaluations or arithmetic introduce perturbations \(\delta_j\), the extrapolated error instead has the form
\[
e^+=q(A)e_0+\sum_j C_j\delta_j
      =\sum_j C_j\delta_j,
\]
which is generally nonzero. Likewise, nonlinear remainder terms, truncated memory, regularization, stagnation, or rank loss can prevent construction of the annihilating polynomial. Consequently minimal-polynomial termination is an exact-arithmetic affine result, not a general finite-precision or nonlinear guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimal-polynomial termination can be destroyed by roundoff, noisy evaluations, nonlinear remainders, memory truncation, regularization, or rank loss.
assumptions_latex: An annihilating polynomial exists for the unperturbed affine model.
At least one arithmetic, oracle, model, or subspace perturbation may be nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbed terminal error need not vanish even when \(q(A)e_0=0\) for the ideal model.

notation.meaning: propagation operator for the j-th perturbation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact polynomial cancellation is generically lost under nonzero perturbations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the exact-arithmetic validity leaf. The qualitative warning is sound, but the displayed perturbation formula introduces unspecified propagation operators C_j and merges roundoff, noisy oracles, nonlinear remainders, truncation, regularization, and rank loss without a defined common model or source.

children.title: Performance-Estimation Parameter Calculus
children.top_down_role: Worst-case analysis and systematic design of relaxation and anchoring schedules.

children.title: Fixed-Point Performance Estimation
children.top_down_role: Finite-dimensional worst-case analysis frameworks for fixed-point residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Performance Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon worst-case residual analysis as a Gram-matrix semidefinite program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a horizon and an algorithm whose iterates are prescribed linear combinations of previously generated points \(x_i\) and oracle values \(g_i=T x_i\). Introduce a fixed point \(x_\star=g_\star\) and impose
\[
\lVert g_i-g_j\rVert^2\leq\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2,
\qquad
\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert^2\leq R^2.
\]
Every squared norm and inner product in these constraints and in the terminal objective \(\lVert x_N-g_N\rVert^2\) is linear in the Gram matrix of the sampled vectors. Maximizing that objective subject to the algorithmic equalities, interpolation inequalities, and Gram-matrix positivity gives a finite semidefinite performance-estimation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-horizon worst-case nonexpansive residual problem becomes an SDP over the Gram matrix of iterates and oracle values.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm has a fixed finite horizon and linear information structure.
\(T\) is nonexpansive and has a fixed point.
The initial squared distance is bounded by \(R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case value of \(\lVert x_N-Tx_N\rVert^2\) admits a finite Gram-matrix semidefinite formulation.

notation.meaning: sampled oracle value T applied to the i-th point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nonexpansive interpolation inequalities and Gram lifting are the standard performance-estimation construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits fixed-point performance estimation. A source is needed to establish whether the listed pairwise nonexpansive interpolation constraints yield an exact finite SDP or only a relaxation under the intended Hilbert-space and dimension assumptions.

children.title: Computer-Assisted Schedule Design
children.top_down_role: Optimization-based discovery of relaxation and anchoring schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Computer-Assisted Schedule Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer optimization of fixed-point schedules using performance-estimation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose a horizon \(N\), an admissible parameter set \(\Theta\), and a parameterized iteration with schedule \(\theta\in\Theta\). For each fixed \(\theta\), construct the fixed-point performance-estimation semidefinite program whose objective bounds \(\lVert x_N-Tx_N\rVert^2\). Solve
\[
\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\ \mathcal W_N(\theta),
\]
where \(\mathcal W_N(\theta)\) is the SDP worst-case value; use global search, verified enumeration, or alternating primal-dual optimization when the outer problem is nonconvex. Return the best schedule together with a feasible dual SDP certificate. Stop when the prescribed outer optimality tolerance and inner feasibility tolerance are met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schedule design minimizes an SDP-computed worst-case residual over admissible anchoring or relaxation parameters and returns a dual performance certificate.
assumptions_latex: A finite parameterized iteration and admissible set \(\Theta\) are specified.
Each fixed schedule has a well-defined performance-estimation SDP.
Numerical feasibility and outer optimality tolerances are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a schedule \(\widehat\theta\) and a dual certificate bounding its worst-case terminal residual by \(\mathcal W_N(\widehat\theta)\).

notation.meaning: vector of anchoring or relaxation parameters
horizon-N worst-case value supplied by performance estimation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: parameterized performance-estimation problems support numerical minimax schedule discovery and dual certification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits computer-assisted schedule design, but no source supports the proposed outer optimization workflow. A feasible dual certificate bounds a fixed schedule under suitable duality conditions; it does not by itself certify global optimality of a nonconvex schedule search, so the certificate and stopping claims require precise sourcing.

children.title: Adaptive Restart Design
children.top_down_role: Worst-case and online perspectives on restart selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Restart Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-triggered geometric restart for an accelerated fixed-point method with unknown effective epoch length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:C\to C\) and \(r(x)=x-Tx\). Choose \(x_0\in C\), \(m_0\in\mathbb N\), \(\gamma>1\), \(\eta\in(0,1)\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At epoch \(j\), initialize the accelerator at \(z_j\), run it for \(m_j\) evaluations, and let \(H_j\) contain the epoch iterates. Set \(z_{j+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in H_j}\|r(x)\|\). If \(\|r(z_{j+1})\|\leq\eta\|r(z_j)\|\), retain \(m_{j+1}=m_j\); otherwise set \(m_{j+1}=\lceil\gamma m_j\rceil\). Restart with cleared history at \(z_{j+1}\), and return the first point satisfying \(\|r(z_{j+1})\|\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restart from the best epoch iterate; retain successful epoch lengths, enlarge unsuccessful ones geometrically, and stop when the residual reaches tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(T:C\to C\) is evaluable on a nonempty set \(C\).
Each finite accelerator epoch is well defined.
Residual norms are available for epoch iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|r(z_{j+1})\|\leq\varepsilon\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the leaf, but no source supports this particular residual trigger, geometric epoch update, or best-iterate restart rule. No termination or worst-case guarantee is asserted.

children.title: Deterministic Inexact Evaluations
children.top_down_role: Controlled deterministic errors in accelerated fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Inexact Evaluations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic error model controlling both individual evaluations and history-induced error amplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the exact map \(T:C\to H\), an inexact evaluation sequence has the form \(\widetilde T_k(x_k)=T(x_k)+e_k\), where \(\|e_k\|\leq\delta_k\). If an accelerated candidate combines evaluations indexed by \(I_k\) with coefficients \(\alpha_{k,i}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_{k,i}=1\) and \(\sum_{i\in I_k}|\alpha_{k,i}|\leq B\), then its injected evaluation error obeys \(\|\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_{k,i}e_i\|\leq B\max_{i\in I_k}\delta_i\). A controlled deterministic regime requires finite \(B\) and either \(\delta_k\to0\) for vanishing local contamination or \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_k<\infty\) for summable perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation errors are bounded, while a uniform coefficient bound prevents residual-history mixing from magnifying them without control.
assumptions_latex: The mixing coefficients have uniformly bounded \(\ell_1\)-norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left\|\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_{k,i}e_i\right\|\leq B\max_{i\in I_k}\delta_i\)

children.title: Stochastic Residual Noise
children.top_down_role: Sampling noise and history contamination in residual-based accelerators.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Residual Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Martingale-difference residual noise with explicit second-moment control and contamination of residual differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\geq0}\) describe the information available before sampling at iteration \(k\). A stochastic residual evaluation is \(\widehat r_k=r(x_k)+\xi_k\), where \(x_k\) is \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable, \(\mathbb E[\xi_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\), and \(\mathbb E[\|\xi_k\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\leq\sigma_k^2\). A stored residual difference satisfies \(\widehat r_i-\widehat r_j=r(x_i)-r(x_j)+\xi_i-\xi_j\); hence every history model built from sampled differences contains correlated noise whenever stored samples share randomness or are selected using later information. Valid stochastic analysis must retain this filtration dependence rather than treating history columns as independent observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual samples are conditionally unbiased with bounded variance, but their stored differences may be correlated through shared randomness and adaptive history selection.
assumptions_latex: The noise has a finite conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\xi_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0,\qquad \mathbb E[\|\xi_k\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\leq\sigma_k^2\)

children.title: Finite-Precision Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Rounding-driven rank loss, residual floors, and false progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual floors and numerical rank loss in finite-precision residual-history least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose computed residuals satisfy \(\widehat r_i=r(x_i)+e_i\), and write the exact and computed history matrices as \(R_k=[\Delta r_i]_{i\in I_k}\) and \(\widehat R_k=R_k+E_k\). When \(\sigma_{\min}(R_k)\leq\|E_k\|_2\), the numerical rank of the history is not reliably distinguishable from rank deficiency, so an unregularized mixing solve may produce large coefficients and false predicted reduction. Moreover, if \(\|r(x_k)\|\leq\|e_k\|\), the computed residual cannot reliably certify further progress. Thus stable execution requires rank truncation or regularization and a stopping floor commensurate with the residual-evaluation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stagnation begins when rounding matches the residual or overwhelms the smallest history singular value, making progress and rank numerically unreliable.
assumptions_latex: Residuals and history differences are computed in finite precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\min}(R_k)\leq\|E_k\|_2\quad\text{or}\quad\|r(x_k)\|\leq\|e_k\|\)

notation.meaning: rounding perturbation of the residual-history matrix
smallest singular value of the exact history matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but the rank-reliability threshold, coefficient behavior, residual floor, and prescribed remedies need a numerical linear algebra or finite-precision source; constants depend on the rank criterion and implementation.

children.title: Matrix-Free Residual Evaluation

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Residual Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-only Anderson-type mixing without forming a Jacobian or matrix representation of the fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given oracle access to \(T:C\to C\), compute \(y_i=T(x_i)\) and \(r_i=x_i-y_i\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(I_k\subseteq\{0,\ldots,k\}\) with \(k\in I_k\), solve \(\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i=1}\|\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i r_i\|\), and set \(x_{k+1}=\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_{k,i}y_i\). Store only selected vectors and inner products needed by the small least-squares problem. Stop when \(\|r_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), returning \(x_k\). The procedure uses evaluations of \(T\) but neither forms nor applies a Jacobian of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the operator, form residual vectors, solve a small affine mixing problem, and update using stored images without constructing a Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is an affine subset of a Hilbert space.
The oracle returns \(T(x)\) for each requested \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_{k,i}T(x_i),\qquad \sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_{k,i}=1\)

children.title: Block Residual Histories
children.top_down_role: History organization for maps with coupled block residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Residual Histories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-row representation of one fixed-point residual history and its weighted mixing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the residual space decompose orthogonally as \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_p\), with block projections \(P_b:H\to H_b\). For a residual-history matrix \(R_k=[\Delta r_{k-m},\ldots,\Delta r_{k-1}]\), define \(R_k^{(b)}=P_bR_k\) and \(r_k^{(b)}=P_br_k\). For weights \(w_b>0\), the block mixing objective has the exact representation \[\sum_{b=1}^{p}w_b\|R_k^{(b)}\gamma-r_k^{(b)}\|^2=\|W^{1/2}(R_k\gamma-r_k)\|^2,\] where \(W\) acts as \(w_bI\) on \(H_b\). Thus blocks may be stored and reduced separately while defining one global coefficient vector \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition one residual history by variable blocks; weighted block objectives equal a single global weighted least-squares model with shared coefficients.
assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_p\) is an orthogonal direct sum.

children.title: Batched Residual Histories

knowledge_statements.title: Batched Residual Histories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-diagonal representation of independent, simultaneously processed fixed-point histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B\) independent fixed-point instances, let \(R_k^{(b)}\) and \(r_k^{(b)}\) be the active history matrix and current residual of instance \(b\). Define \(\mathcal R_k=\operatorname{diag}(R_k^{(1)},\ldots,R_k^{(B)})\), \(\mathcal r_k=(r_k^{(1)},\ldots,r_k^{(B)})\), and \(\gamma=(\gamma^{(1)},\ldots,\gamma^{(B)})\). Then \[\|\mathcal R_k\gamma-\mathcal r_k\|^2=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\|R_k^{(b)}\gamma^{(b)}-r_k^{(b)}\|^2.\] Consequently, an uncoupled batched history solve is exactly separable across instances even when its matrix operations are executed as one batch; each instance retains its own coefficients and restart state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent histories form a block-diagonal least-squares problem, enabling batched execution without mathematically coupling coefficients or restart states.
assumptions_latex: All instance residual spaces are Hilbert spaces.
The batch objective contains no cross-instance regularizer or shared constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\gamma}\|\mathcal R_k\gamma-\mathcal r_k\|^2=\prod_{b=1}^{B}\operatorname*{argmin}_{\gamma^{(b)}}\|R_k^{(b)}\gamma^{(b)}-r_k^{(b)}\|^2\)

children.title: Cross-Instance History Coupling

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Instance History Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-regularized coupling of aligned history coefficients across related fixed-point instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(B\) instances use aligned histories of common width \(m\). Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be an undirected weighted graph relating instances. Cross-instance coefficient coupling is represented by \[\min_{\gamma^{(1)},\ldots,\gamma^{(B)}}\ \sum_{b=1}^{B}\|R_k^{(b)}\gamma^{(b)}-r_k^{(b)}\|^2+\lambda\sum_{(b,c)\in E}w_{bc}\|\gamma^{(b)}-\gamma^{(c)}\|^2,\] possibly subject to identical affine constraints on each coefficient vector. With stacked coefficients \(\Gamma\), the coupling term equals \(\lambda\|(L_G^{1/2}\otimes I_m)\Gamma\|^2\). Setting \(\lambda=0\) recovers independent batched histories; positive \(\lambda\) transfers history information only along graph edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Related instances can share information by graph-regularizing differences between aligned mixing coefficients; zero coupling recovers independent batched solves.
assumptions_latex: All active histories have common width \(m\).
Coupled coefficient vectors use compatible constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda\sum_{(b,c)\in E}w_{bc}\|\gamma^{(b)}-\gamma^{(c)}\|^2=\lambda\|(L_G^{1/2}\otimes I_m)\Gamma\|^2\)

children.title: Synchronous Parallel Mixing

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronous Parallel Mixing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collective formation and solution of a row-distributed residual-history least-squares model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the residual and history matrix by workers as \(r=(r^{(1)},\ldots,r^{(p)})\) and \(R=[(R^{(1)})^\top,\ldots,(R^{(p)})^\top]^\top\). At a synchronization point, worker \(b\) forms \(G_b=(R^{(b)})^*R^{(b)}\) and \(g_b=(R^{(b)})^*r^{(b)}\). A collective reduction computes \(G=\sum_{b=1}^{p}G_b=R^*R\) and \(g=\sum_{b=1}^{p}g_b=R^*r\). The workers solve the same regularized system \((G+\lambda I)\gamma=g\), broadcast \(\gamma\), and simultaneously form their local blocks of the mixed iterate. Stop collectively when the reduced residual norm meets the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers reduce local Gram data, solve one shared small mixing system, broadcast its coefficients, and update all residual blocks synchronously.
assumptions_latex: All workers use the same synchronized history columns.
Collective reductions are exact at the stated arithmetic level.

children.title: Asynchronous History Use

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous History Use
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Version-tagged residual mixing from asynchronously produced, possibly delayed operator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each worker reads a version \(v_i\), evaluates \(y_i=T(x_{v_i})\), forms \(r_i=x_{v_i}-y_i\), and submits the tagged triple \((v_i,x_{v_i},r_i)\). The coordinator selects a finite history \(I_k\) whose delays satisfy \(0\leq k-v_i\leq\tau\), discards duplicate or incompatible tags, and solves \(\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i=1}\|\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i r_i\|\). It forms the candidate \(z_{k+1}=\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_{k,i}T(x_{v_i})\), validates or damps it against the current residual, publishes the accepted version, and stops when a current, not stale, residual meets tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers submit versioned residuals; the coordinator mixes only bounded-delay records and validates the candidate using a current residual.
assumptions_latex: Every stored evaluation is tagged with the iterate version it used.
Accepted history delays are bounded by \(\tau<\infty\).
A current residual evaluation is available for acceptance and stopping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{k+1}=\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_{k,i}T(x_{v_i}),\qquad 0\leq k-v_i\leq\tau\)

notation.meaning: iterate version used by evaluation i

children.title: Stale-History Effects
children.top_down_role: Acceleration behavior when stored residuals correspond to outdated states.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale-History Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative residual mismatch and coefficient amplification caused by delayed history entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be \(q\)-Lipschitz and let \(r=I-T\). For any current iterate \(x_k\) and stale iterate \(x_{k-d}\), \[\|r(x_k)-r(x_{k-d})\|\leq(1+q)\|x_k-x_{k-d}\|.\] Therefore, replacing current residuals in an affine model by stale residuals with coefficients \(\alpha_i\) introduces mismatch at most \((1+q)\sum_i|\alpha_i|\|x_k-x_{v_i}\|\). Delay alone is consequently insufficient to control contamination: stability also depends on iterate drift and the coefficient \(\ell_1\)-norm. Large extrapolative coefficients can amplify small individual stale-history errors into a large model error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stale residual differs from the current residual in proportion to iterate drift, and extrapolative mixing coefficients amplify the aggregate mismatch.
assumptions_latex: Stored residual \(i\) was evaluated at version \(v_i\leq k\).
The history contains finitely many coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left\|\sum_i\alpha_i\bigl(r(x_{v_i})-r(x_k)\bigr)\right\|\leq(1+q)\sum_i|\alpha_i|\|x_{v_i}-x_k\|\)

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the fixed-point map

children.title: Delay-Tolerance Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits beyond which delayed or inconsistent histories cease to provide reliable acceleration.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay-Tolerance Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded delays defeat general convergence guarantees even for scalar contractive fixed-point maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the scalar contraction \(T(x)=qx\) with \(0<q<1\), whose unique fixed point is \(0\), and the fully delayed iteration \(x_{k+1}=T(x_{k-\tau_k})\). If delays are unbounded, convergence need not occur: choose \(\tau_k=k\) and \(x_0\neq0\). Then every update reads \(x_0\), so \(x_{k+1}=qx_0\) for all \(k\geq0\), and the sequence does not converge to the fixed point. Thus a uniform delay bound, or a comparably strong condition ensuring that obsolete states eventually cease to be used, is necessary for convergence guarantees covering all admissible asynchronous schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without bounded or vanishingly obsolete reads, even a scalar contraction can repeatedly use the initial state and fail to approach its fixed point.

children.title: Iteration Count versus Work Complexity
children.top_down_role: Comparison of residual progress with added mixing and linear-algebra costs.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to X\) is a fixed-point map on a normed space, and both compared methods use the same residual and accuracy target.
Each method reaches the target in finitely many iterations, with measurable setup and per-iteration work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) accelerates \(B\) in work at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(W_A(\varepsilon)<W_B(\varepsilon)\), irrespective of whether \(N_A(\varepsilon)<N_B(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: First iteration satisfying the common accuracy test for method M
Setup work plus accumulated iteration work

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work-based acceleration for two fixed-point implementations under a common stopping test.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Computational complexity via flop count p. 99

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For method \(M\in\{A,B\}\), let \(N_M(\varepsilon)\) be the first iteration satisfying a common accuracy test at tolerance \(\varepsilon\), and define total work by \[W_M(\varepsilon)=w_M^{\mathrm{setup}}+\sum_{k=0}^{N_M(\varepsilon)-1}w_{M,k}.\] An iteration-count gain occurs when \(N_A(\varepsilon)<N_B(\varepsilon)\), whereas a work-complexity gain occurs when \(W_A(\varepsilon)<W_B(\varepsilon)\). Thus reduced iteration count is insufficient for computational acceleration: the added mixing, storage maintenance, least-squares solution, or other linear-algebra work must not exceed the work saved by the omitted baseline iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration in iteration count is computationally meaningful only when setup and all added per-iteration costs still yield lower total work at the chosen tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Count versus Work Complexity

children.title: Transient versus Asymptotic Gain
children.top_down_role: Separation of early behavior from eventual rate improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Transient versus Asymptotic Gain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates finite-horizon residual improvement from eventual root-linear rate improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For methods \(A\) and \(B\), let \((r_k^A)_{k\ge 0}\) and \((r_k^B)_{k\ge 0}\) be nonnegative residual sequences converging to zero. For a horizon \(K\in\mathbb{N}_0\), a transient gain at \(K\) is expressed by \(r_K^A<r_K^B\), or by a separately specified finite-horizon aggregate. Define the upper asymptotic root factors by \[\rho_M=\limsup_{k\to\infty}(r_k^M)^{1/k},\qquad M\in\{A,B\}.\] An asymptotic gain means \(\rho_A<\rho_B\). Neither comparison implies the other: finite startup overhead or unfavorable initial coefficients can hide a better asymptotic factor, while an early residual reduction can coexist with an equal or worse eventual factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Early residual improvement and better eventual convergence rate are distinct properties; startup behavior can conceal asymptotic gain, and transient gain need not persist.
assumptions_latex: The compared residual sequences are nonnegative and converge to zero.
The same residual normalization and iteration index are used for both methods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite-horizon gain and an asymptotic-rate gain are logically independent; either may hold without the other.

notation.meaning: Residual of method M after iteration k

children.title: Metric-Conditioning Assessment
children.top_down_role: Dependence of observed acceleration on metric and conditioning choices.

children.title: Scaling Effects
children.top_down_role: Dependence of observed acceleration on variable, residual, or metric scaling.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaling preserves fixed points by conjugacy but changes Euclidean residual magnitudes and induced operator conditioning through \(S^{\mathsf T}S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate scaling effects on fixed points, residual norms, and conditioning.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the coordinate change \(y=Sx\), define \(F_S(y)=SF(S^{-1}y)\). Then \[y=F_S(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S^{-1}y=F(S^{-1}y),\] so scaling preserves the fixed-point set up to the bijection \(S\). For \(r(x)=F(x)-x\), the scaled residual is \(r_S(y)=Sr(S^{-1}y)\), and hence \[\|r_S(Sx)\|_2^2=r(x)^{\mathsf T}S^{\mathsf T}Sr(x).\] Consequently, scaling can alter measured residual progress and norm-dependent conditioning even though it does not alter the underlying fixed-point solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular coordinate scaling preserves fixed points but changes residual magnitudes and norm-dependent conditioning, so apparent acceleration may depend on the selected scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Effects

children.title: Preconditioning Effects
children.top_down_role: Dependence of acceleration gains on transformations that alter effective conditioning.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable near a fixed point \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Preconditioning preserves the fixed points and changes the local linear factor from \(J\) to \(I-P(I-J)\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the original map at the fixed point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Left preconditioning of the fixed-point residual and its local convergence factor.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the preconditioned map by \[G_P(x)=x+P(F(x)-x).\] Since \(P\) is nonsingular, \(G_P(x)=x\) holds exactly when \(F(x)=x\); thus preconditioning preserves the fixed-point set. If \(J=DF(x^\star)\), then \[DG_P(x^\star)=I-P(I-J).\] Therefore the local asymptotic behavior can be improved or degraded according to the spectral radius and nonnormality of \(I-P(I-J)\). Any iteration reduction must be assessed together with the cost of applying \(P\) and constructing or updating it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular residual preconditioner preserves solutions but changes the local iteration matrix, potentially improving convergence at the cost of applying and maintaining the preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioning Effects

children.title: Scaling–Preconditioning Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined influence of metric normalization and conditioning transformations on comparative performance.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), \(S\), and \(P\) satisfy the assumptions of the scaling and preconditioning records.
The transformed preconditioner is represented exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistent transformation \(P_S=SPS^{-1}\) makes scaled preconditioning conjugate to original preconditioning, preserving eigenvalues but not normwise or implementation costs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistent coordinate transformation of residual preconditioners.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_S(y)=SF(S^{-1}y)\) and transform the preconditioner consistently as \(P_S=SPS^{-1}\). The scaled, preconditioned map satisfies \[y+P_S(F_S(y)-y)=S\bigl(S^{-1}y+P(F(S^{-1}y)-S^{-1}y)\bigr)=SG_P(S^{-1}y).\] Hence the two preconditioned iterations are conjugate. Their local Jacobians are similar and have identical eigenvalues and spectral radii. Nevertheless, Euclidean residual histories, nonnormality measures, sparsity, numerical stability, and the cost of applying \(P_S\) may differ, so scaling and preconditioning cannot be assessed independently at the implementation level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a preconditioner is transformed consistently with the coordinates, local spectra are unchanged, but normwise behavior, sparsity, stability, and application cost can still change.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling–Preconditioning Interaction

children.title: Accuracy-Target Stopping Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Acceleration value across different solver-accuracy targets.

children.title: Accuracy-Target Effects
children.top_down_role: Variation in acceleration value across coarse, moderate, or stringent accuracy targets.

assumptions_latex: Both methods use the same nonnegative normalized residual sequence definition.
Each target tolerance is attained in finitely many iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordering of \(N_A(\varepsilon)\) and \(N_B(\varepsilon)\) may change with \(\varepsilon\); acceleration is therefore target-specific unless uniform dominance is established.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of observed iteration acceleration on the requested residual tolerance.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For method \(M\), define the hitting time \[N_M(\varepsilon)=\min\{k\ge 0:r_k^M\le\varepsilon\}.\] An acceleration claim at target \(\varepsilon\) is the comparison \(N_A(\varepsilon)<N_B(\varepsilon)\), possibly augmented by work or time costs. Residual curves can cross, so this ordering need not persist as \(\varepsilon\) varies. Uniform iteration acceleration on an interval \(E\subset(0,\infty)\) requires \(N_A(\varepsilon)\le N_B(\varepsilon)\) for every \(\varepsilon\in E\), with strict inequality for at least one target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual curves can cross, so one method may win at a loose tolerance and lose at a strict one; acceleration claims must specify the target accuracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-Target Effects

children.title: Stopping-Regime Effects
children.top_down_role: Influence of termination criteria on measured solver advantage.

knowledge_statements.title: Stopping-Regime Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effects of residual, step, budget, and stagnation stopping rules on measured performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each method \(M\in\{A,B\}\) and stopping regime \(j\), let \(C_{M,j}(k)\) be the Boolean stopping predicate after iteration \(k\in\mathbb{N}_0\), and define \[N_{M,j}=\min\{k\ge 0:C_{M,j}(k)=\mathrm{true}\}.\] Different regimes may use an absolute residual, relative residual, step size, objective change, stagnation test, iteration budget, or time budget. Because these predicates need not first become true at the same iteration, they can induce different iteration counts and accumulated costs. The iteration-count ranking of \(A\) and \(B\) is invariant between regimes \(i\) and \(j\) exactly when the signs of \(N_{A,i}-N_{B,i}\) and \(N_{A,j}-N_{B,j}\) agree, with ties treated explicitly. Quantitative relations between criteria can support comparisons only after their thresholds and their validity over all relevant method histories are specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different stopping rules can stop the same methods at different times and can reverse their measured ranking; invariance requires the method ordering to be preserved under the specified regimes.
assumptions_latex: For every compared method and regime, the stopping predicate produces a Boolean decision from the method history and the stopping time is finite.
All compared runs share the same problem instance, initialization, and implementation environment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Performance under one stopping regime does not determine performance under another unless the resulting stopping times or costs preserve the compared ordering.

notation.meaning: Stopping predicate for method M under regime j after iteration k
Stopping iteration for method M under regime j
Measured accumulated cost for method M through stopping under regime j

children.title: Accuracy–Stopping Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Changes in comparative acceleration conclusions caused by pairing different targets with termination criteria.

assumptions_latex: For every compared method, the stopping time is finite at both targets.
The stopping predicate and normalization are fixed while the target changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Large \(|S_M(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)|\) indicates target-sensitive stopping cost, while ranking stability requires the pairwise performance difference to retain its sign.

notation.meaning: Stopping cost of method M at target epsilon

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-difference sensitivity of stopping cost and method ranking to target accuracy.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_M(\varepsilon)>0\) denote the iteration count, work, or wall-clock cost incurred by method \(M\) under a fixed stopping predicate with target \(\varepsilon\). For distinct targets \(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\), define finite log-sensitivity by \[S_M(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)=\frac{\log C_M(\varepsilon_2)-\log C_M(\varepsilon_1)}{\log \varepsilon_2-\log \varepsilon_1}.\] Pairwise ranking sensitivity is detected when \(D_{A,B}(\varepsilon)=C_A(\varepsilon)-C_B(\varepsilon)\) changes sign over the target range. This separates sensitivity of an individual method from sensitivity of the comparative acceleration claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accuracy-stopping sensitivity measures how rapidly stopping cost changes with tolerance and whether changing that tolerance reverses the ranking of two methods.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy–Stopping Sensitivity

children.top_down_role: System-level evaluation beyond sequential arithmetic counts.

children.title: Wall-Clock Metrics
children.top_down_role: End-to-end elapsed-time evaluation of accelerated solver execution.

assumptions_latex: Timing uses a fixed hardware, software, parallelism, and synchronization configuration.
The measured interval and stopping criterion are identical across compared methods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Wall-clock acceleration at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) means \(T_A(\varepsilon)<T_B(\varepsilon)\) under the same declared execution environment.

notation.meaning: Total elapsed time to the stopping target

knowledge_statements.scope_note: End-to-end elapsed-time metric under a fixed execution environment.

source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Computational complexity via flop count p. 99

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For method \(M\) stopped at target \(\varepsilon\), its end-to-end wall-clock metric is \[T_M(\varepsilon)=t_M^{\mathrm{setup}}+\sum_{k=0}^{N_M(\varepsilon)-1}t_{M,k}^{\mathrm{crit}}+t_M^{\mathrm{finalize}},\] where each critical-path term includes computation, memory stalls, communication, synchronization, and runtime overhead occurring within the measured interval. Timing must specify hardware, process and thread counts, software configuration, warm-up policy, and aggregation across repeated runs. Wall-clock acceleration is the inequality \(T_A(\varepsilon)<T_B(\varepsilon)\) under the same declared environment and stopping criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wall-clock performance is end-to-end elapsed time to a common target, including setup, critical-path computation, communication, synchronization, and finalization under a fixed environment.
knowledge_statements.title: Wall-Clock Metrics

children.title: Memory Metrics
children.top_down_role: Storage costs associated with residual histories, auxiliary states, or solver workspaces.

assumptions_latex: All storage attributable to the method is included under a fixed accounting convention.
Compared methods solve the same instance to the same stopping target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Method \(A\) has a peak-memory advantage at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(M_A^{\mathrm{peak}}(\varepsilon)<M_B^{\mathrm{peak}}(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: Cumulative allocated or transferred storage volume

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak and cumulative storage metrics for accelerated fixed-point implementations.

source_refs.locator: 6.2 Extended coordinate-friendly operators and exclusive memory access p. 142

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m_M(t)\) be the bytes of live method-attributable storage at time \(t\), including iterates, residual histories, mixing coefficients, factorizations, communication buffers, and replicated data. The peak-memory metric to target \(\varepsilon\) is \[M_M^{\mathrm{peak}}(\varepsilon)=\max_{0\le t\le T_M(\varepsilon)}m_M(t).\] A distinct cumulative-volume metric may count all bytes allocated, read, written, or transferred during the run. Peak storage and cumulative volume must not be conflated: an accelerator can increase retained history while decreasing cumulative traffic through fewer iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory assessment distinguishes maximum simultaneously live storage from cumulative allocation or traffic; acceleration may improve one metric while worsening the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory Metrics

children.title: Communication Metrics
children.top_down_role: Data-movement costs across workers, devices, or memory levels.

assumptions_latex: The processor or worker partition and communication interface are fixed.
All messages induced by setup and iterations through the common stopping target are counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Communication performance must report at least rounds and volume, because neither message count nor transferred words alone determines critical-path cost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Latency, message-count, and bandwidth measures through a common stopping target.

source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods
Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed worker partition, communication to tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is summarized by the tuple \[(R_M(\varepsilon),Q_M(\varepsilon),V_M(\varepsilon)),\] comprising critical-path communication rounds, messages, and transferred words. In the latency-bandwidth model with nonnegative parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), an estimated critical-path communication time is \[T_M^{\mathrm{comm}}(\varepsilon)=\alpha Q_M(\varepsilon)+\beta V_M(\varepsilon),\] with synchronization delays reported separately or included explicitly. Accelerated mixing can reduce rounds by lowering iteration count while increasing message size through history exchange or collective linear algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication metrics count rounds, messages, and transferred volume; fewer iterations can reduce synchronization while larger mixing operations increase per-round traffic.
knowledge_statements.title: Communication Metrics

children.title: System-Metric Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparative assessment when improvements in one system metric increase costs in another.

assumptions_latex: All methods are evaluated on the same problem, target, and execution environment.
Each reported cost component is measured under a common accounting convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A method is system-dominated only when another method is no worse in every reported metric and strictly better in at least one.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto comparison of time, work, memory, and communication costs.

source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Computational complexity via flop count p. 99
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At target \(\varepsilon\), collect system costs into \[c_M(\varepsilon)=(T_M,W_M,M_M^{\mathrm{peak}},R_M,Q_M,V_M),\] with all components interpreted as costs to minimize. Method \(A\) Pareto-dominates method \(B\) when \(c_A(\varepsilon)\preceq c_B(\varepsilon)\) componentwise and at least one inequality is strict. If neither vector dominates the other, declaring a unique winner requires an explicit scalarization, resource budget, or lexicographic priority. Thus a reduction in iterations or flops alone does not establish system-level acceleration when memory, communication, or critical-path time increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: System-level acceleration is multiobjective: one method dominates only if it is no worse in every reported cost and strictly better in at least one.
knowledge_statements.title: System-Metric Tradeoffs

children.title: Accelerator Selection-Hybridization System
children.top_down_role: Selection and composition of baseline, relaxed, anchored, extrapolated, and Anderson modes.

children.title: Baseline–Accelerator Switching
children.top_down_role: Runtime switching between a reliable base iteration and an accelerated mode.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(T:X\to X\), \(x_0\in X\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(K\in\mathbb N_0\).
For each \(k\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\), the accelerator returns \((y_k,\widehat s_{k+1})=A_k(x_k,s_k)\).
The safeguard \(G_k(x_k,y_k)\in\{0,1\}\) and state initializer \(s_{\mathrm{init}}:X\to S\) are computable, where \(S\) is the accelerator-state space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the first \(x_k\) satisfying \(\|T(x_k)-x_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), or returns \(x_K\) after exactly \(K\) updates if no tested iterate satisfies the tolerance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded runtime switching between an accelerated candidate and the unrelaxed fixed-point step.

source_refs.locator: 12.3 When does an acceleration accelerate? p. 260
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(s_0\in S\). For \(k=0,\ldots,K\), return \(x_k\) if \(\|T(x_k)-x_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(x_K\) if \(k=K\) and the residual test fails. Otherwise compute \((y_k,\widehat s_{k+1})=A_k(x_k,s_k)\). If \(G_k(x_k,y_k)=1\), set \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) and \(s_{k+1}=\widehat s_{k+1}\). If \(G_k(x_k,y_k)=0\), set \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) and \(s_{k+1}=s_{\mathrm{init}}(x_{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test the current residual at each iteration. Accept an accelerated candidate only when the safeguard passes; otherwise take the baseline fixed-point step and reinitialize the accelerator. Return the first iterate meeting the tolerance, or the iterate obtained after the prescribed number of updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Baseline–Accelerator Switching

children.title: Accelerator State-Reinitialization Policies
children.top_down_role: Cross-family policies for discarding momentum, anchors, or residual histories.

children.title: Scheduled Restart Policies
children.top_down_role: Restart choices based on predetermined iteration, epoch, or resource schedules.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(T:X\to X\), \(x_0\in X\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(K\in\mathbb N_0\).
The accelerator state lies in a space \(S\), the initializer is \(s_{\mathrm{init}}:X\to S\), and each update returns \((x_{k+1},\widehat s_{k+1})=A_k(x_k,s_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The current iterate is retained and the accelerator state is reinitialized after each completed block of \(q\) updates.

notation.meaning: state initializer at a retained iterate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic periodic restart independent of observed progress.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(s_0=s_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)\). For \(k=0,\ldots,K\), return \(x_k\) if \(\|T(x_k)-x_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(x_K\) if \(k=K\) and the test fails. Otherwise compute \((x_{k+1},\widehat s_{k+1})=A_k(x_k,s_k)\). If \(q\mid(k+1)\), retain \(x_{k+1}\) and set \(s_{k+1}=s_{\mathrm{init}}(x_{k+1})\); otherwise set \(s_{k+1}=\widehat s_{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run the accelerator in blocks of a prescribed positive-integer length. After each complete block, retain the current iterate and reinitialize the accelerator state. Stop at the first residual-feasible iterate or after the prescribed number of updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Scheduled Restart Policies

children.title: Triggered Reset Policies
children.top_down_role: Reset choices activated by observed deterioration, instability, or loss of progress.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(T:X\to X\), \(x_0\in X\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(K\in\mathbb N_0\).
The accelerator state lies in a space \(S\), the diagnostics lie in a set \(Z\), and \(z_0\in Z\) is an initial diagnostic.
For each \(k\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\), the accelerator returns \((x_{k+1},\widehat s_{k+1},z_{k+1})=A_k(x_k,s_k)\), and the computable trigger satisfies \(H_k:Z^{k+2}\to\{0,1\}\).
A state initializer \(s_{\mathrm{init}}:X\to S\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(H_k(z_0,\ldots,z_{k+1})=1\), the iterate \(x_{k+1}\) is retained and the next update starts from \(s_{\mathrm{init}}(x_{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-driven state reset based on a computable robustness diagnostic.

source_refs.locator: 12.3 When does an acceleration accelerate? p. 260

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(s_0=s_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)\) and \(z_0\in Z\). For \(k=0,\ldots,K\), return \(x_k\) if \(\|T(x_k)-x_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(x_K\) if \(k=K\) and the test fails. Otherwise compute \((x_{k+1},\widehat s_{k+1},z_{k+1})=A_k(x_k,s_k)\). If \(H_k(z_0,\ldots,z_{k+1})=1\), retain \(x_{k+1}\) and set \(s_{k+1}=s_{\mathrm{init}}(x_{k+1})\); otherwise set \(s_{k+1}=\widehat s_{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After each accelerated update, evaluate the specified trigger on the available diagnostic history. When it fires, retain the new iterate but reinitialize the accelerator state before the next update. Stop at the residual tolerance or update limit.

children.title: Momentum-State Discard
children.top_down_role: Policies governing removal of accumulated momentum or extrapolation state.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed vector space, \(T:X\to X\), \(x_0\in X\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(K\in\mathbb N_0\).
The momentum coefficients satisfy \(\beta_k\in\mathbb R\) for \(k\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(k\in R\), replacing the stored predecessor by \(x_k\) gives \(x_k-x_{k-1}=0\) in that update and hence \(y_k=x_k\), independently of \(\beta_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Momentum-state discard for a two-state inertial fixed-point iteration.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_{-1}=x_0\). For \(k=0,\ldots,K\), return \(x_k\) if \(\|T(x_k)-x_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(x_K\) if \(k=K\) and the test fails. If \(k\in R\), replace the stored predecessor by \(x_{k-1}\leftarrow x_k\). Then form \(y_k=x_k+\beta_k(x_k-x_{k-1})\) and set \(x_{k+1}=T(y_k)\). At a reset index, this gives \(y_k=x_k\), so the update contains no inherited momentum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each reset index, replace the stored predecessor by the current iterate before forming the inertial extrapolation. This makes the momentum difference zero for that update. Stop at the first residual-feasible iterate or after the prescribed number of updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Momentum-State Discard

children.title: Anchor-State Reinitialization
children.top_down_role: Policies governing replacement of anchors or reference states.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a convex subset of a normed vector space, \(T:X\to X\), \(x_0\in X\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(K\in\mathbb N_0\).
The within-epoch weights satisfy \(\alpha_j\in[0,1]\) for every \(j\in\mathbb N_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At each \(k\in R\), the reset retains \(x_k\), replaces the anchor by \(x_k\), and restarts the local weight index at \(j=0\).

notation.meaning: weight within the current restart epoch

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anchor-state reinitialization for a Halpern-type fixed-point acceleration.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(a=x_0\) and \(j=0\). For \(k=0,\ldots,K\), return \(x_k\) if \(\|T(x_k)-x_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(x_K\) if \(k=K\) and the test fails. If \(k\in R\), retain \(x_k\), set \(a=x_k\), and reset \(j=0\). Compute \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_j a+(1-\alpha_j)T(x_k)\), then replace \(j\) by \(j+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a reset index, retain the current iterate, make it the new anchor, and restart the within-epoch weight counter. Continue the Halpern-type updates until the residual tolerance or update limit is reached.

children.title: Residual-History Flush
children.top_down_role: Policies governing partial or complete removal of stored residual histories.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed vector space, \(T:X\to X\), \(x_0\in X\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(K\in\mathbb N_0\).
The accelerator constructs candidates from stored pairs \((x_i,r_i)\), where \(r_i=T(x_i)-x_i\).
The history bound satisfies \(m\in\mathbb N\), and the reset indices satisfy \(R\subseteq\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After a flush at \(k\in R\), no stored pair with index \(i<k\) is available to any later accelerated combination unless that data is generated and stored again.

notation.meaning: fixed-point residual at the current iterate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-history flush for a multisecant or Anderson-type fixed-point accelerator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal H=\varnothing\). For \(k=0,\ldots,K\), compute \(r_k=T(x_k)-x_k\). Return \(x_k\) if \(\|r_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(x_K\) if \(k=K\) and the test fails. If \(k\in R\), replace \(\mathcal H\) by \(\varnothing\). If \(\mathcal H=\varnothing\), set \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\); otherwise construct \(x_{k+1}\) by the specified accelerator using only pairs in \(\mathcal H\cup\{(x_k,r_k)\}\). Finally replace \(\mathcal H\) by at most the newest \(m\) pairs from \(\mathcal H\cup\{(x_k,r_k)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a bounded history of iterate-residual pairs. At a flush index, delete the entire history before constructing the next candidate, so that the next step is unaccelerated and later accelerated steps can use only subsequently accumulated history.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-History Flush

children.title: Nested Outer Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Outer acceleration applied to inner fixed-point or splitting solvers.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(T:X\to X\), \(x_0\in X\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(K\in\mathbb N_0\).
For each \(k\in\{0,\ldots,K\}\), \(\eta_k>0\) and the inner solver returns \(u_k=I_{\eta_k}(x_k)\) satisfying \(\|u_k-T(x_k)\|\leq\eta_k\).
For each \(k\in\{0,\ldots,K\}\), a computable nonnegative residual estimator \(\rho_k(x_k,u_k)\) is specified.
For each \(k\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\), the outer accelerator returns \((x_{k+1},s_{k+1})=A_k(x_k,u_k,s_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the first \(x_k\) for which \(\rho_k(x_k,u_k)\leq\varepsilon\), or returns \(x_K\) after \(K\) outer updates, with every \(u_k\) produced at its prescribed inner tolerance \(\eta_k\).

notation.meaning: inner approximation to the fixed-point-map image
inner accuracy at outer iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inexact outer acceleration wrapped around an inner fixed-point or splitting solve; the stopping rule concerns the specified estimator and does not assert convergence to an exact fixed point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial outer state \(s_0\). For \(k=0,\ldots,K\), compute \(u_k=I_{\eta_k}(x_k)\). Return \(x_k\) if \(\rho_k(x_k,u_k)\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(x_K\) if \(k=K\) and the test fails. Otherwise compute \((x_{k+1},s_{k+1})=A_k(x_k,u_k,s_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each outer iteration, use the inner solver to approximate the fixed-point-map image at the prescribed accuracy. Test the specified residual estimator, and, if it fails, pass the approximate image to the outer accelerator. Return the first iterate passing the test or the iterate obtained after the prescribed number of outer updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Outer Acceleration
